title: A nuclear-quantum-corrected machine-learning potential reveals quantum-enhanced hydrogen segregation at general grain boundaries in alpha-iron
abstract: Atomistic descriptions of hydrogen diffusion and trapping at defects are essential for understanding hydrogen embrittlement. As the lightest solute in metals, hydrogen exhibits nuclear quantum effects that alter these processes even at room temperature. Explicit treatment of such effects is computationally demanding, limiting large-scale simulations of complex environments. Here, we use an Fe-H machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) based on the performant implementation of the atomic cluster expansion (PACE), covering diverse Fe-H environments, and relabel the training configurations underpinning its transferability with quantum mean forces from centroid-constrained path-integral molecular dynamics at 300 K. This yields a nuclear-quantum-corrected PACE (NQC-PACE) without additional density functional theory calculations. At parent PACE, NQC-PACE describes nuclear quantum effects on hydrogen trapping at vacancies, dislocations, surfaces and general grain boundaries, H-H interactions, and diffusion in alpha-Fe. Grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations show nuclear quantum effects markedly enhance hydrogen segregation at general grain boundaries and trapping behaviour in closer agreement with experimental trends. This enhancement arises from selective quantum stabilisation of open, anisotropically soft local environments. Our framework uses finite-temperature quantum mean forces to relabel the configurational space covered by an MLIP, enabling large-scale analysis of complex materials where light-element quantum effects matter.
summary: The authors developed a Nuclear-Quantum-Corrected Machine-Learning Potential (NQC-PACE) for the Fe-H system. This potential incorporates difficult-to-calculate nuclear quantum effects by relabeling an existing MLIP using Path-Integral Molecular Dynamics data. The results demonstrate that these quantum corrections significantly enhance hydrogen segregation at grain boundaries, offering a computationally tractable tool for studying light element behavior in complex materials.
main_problem: Accurately simulating hydrogen diffusion and trapping at defects in iron while incorporating computationally demanding nuclear quantum effects (NQE) into large-scale simulations.
main_result: The developed NQC-PACE potential shows that NQE markedly enhance hydrogen segregation at general grain boundaries, providing a significant improvement over classical potentials.
method: A novel framework was created by relabeling the configurational space of an existing Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential (MLIP) using quantum mean forces derived from Path-Integral Molecular Dynamics (PIMD).
model_or_system: The system is hydrogen dissolved in alpha-iron ($\alpha$-Fe), focusing on defects like vacancies, dislocations, and general grain boundaries. The model uses an MLIP trained via the atomic cluster expansion (PACE) and corrected to NQC-PACE.
key_observables: Hydrogen segregation levels, trapping energies, diffusion coefficients ($D$), and comparison of quantum vs. classical binding sites.
important_parameters: Temperature (300 K), light element mass effects (hydrogen), and the configurational space coverage of the parent MLIP.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that relabeling the configurational space with PIMD-derived quantum mean forces is sufficient to incorporate NQE corrections without requiring additional DFT calculations for every new configuration.

paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem (H embrittlement/NQE), details the methodology (PIMD to generate quantum mean forces for MLIP relabeling into NQC-PACE), presents results comparing NQC-PACE against classical potentials, and concludes with implications for large-scale materials simulation.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter, the core technique—using high-level quantum dynamics (PIMD) to parameterize and correct a lower-level, computationally efficient MLIP across vast configurational spaces—is a powerful general methodology relevant to simulating complex quantum many-body systems in materials science.
